title: Not a stiff upper lip
hookLine: in English "stoic" means unfeeling, which isn't what the Stoics meant

cards: Read any sports page and you'll find it. The coach remained stoic after the loss. The widow was stoic at the funeral.
In everyday English, stoic means jaw set, no tears, feelings locked in a box. Stiff upper lip. It's easy to assume that's the whole philosophy.
After more than two weeks on the porch, you already know that's off. Today: how far off, and a future emperor who cried.

teach.b: The confusion has a source. The Stoics' ideal was apatheia, freedom from pathos, the runaway passions we met two weeks ago. English turned that word into apathy, not caring at all, and turned stoic into unfeeling.
But the actual goal was freedom from feelings built on false judgments, with room for good ones: joy, wise wishing, caution.

Epictetus says it directly in his Discourses: a person shouldn't be unfeeling like a statue, but should keep up his natural relationships, as a son, a brother, a father, a citizen. A statue feels nothing.
A Stoic loves his family. Then grief.
Seneca wrote to a friend who had lost someone, and his advice was roughly: let the eyes not be dry, and don't let them flood either; you may weep, just don't wail without end.
In the same letter he confesses that when his own dear friend Annaeus Serenus died, he wept so much that he stands as an example of someone overcome by grief. A Stoic admitting it, in writing.
And a late, not very reliable Roman history tells how young Marcus Aurelius wept at the death of his tutor, and courtiers tried to stop him.
The emperor Antoninus said, roughly: let him be human; neither philosophy nor empire takes away natural feeling. Whether or not it happened just that way, it's how that history remembers him.
You may also meet a newer version online: Stoicism sold as never showing weakness, bottling everything up, or getting the upper hand on people.
Plenty of readers of the old texts point out that it's close to the opposite: feel it first, then choose what to do. In these writers, the Stoic isn't the one with no tears.
It's the one whose tears are honest, and who isn't swept away by them.

how: Stoic practitioners today distinguish apatheia, freedom from runaway passions, from apathy, and allow grief and love their honest place.

o: not caring about anything, the root of apathy
freedom from runaway passions, not from feeling
keeping a calm face whatever you feel inside

p: the English word that took it over
what Epictetus said not to be

s: the Stoics taught people to show no feelings
they aimed at freedom from false-judgment passions, not from feeling.
Seneca admitted he wept heavily for a friend
in a letter on grief, he names Annaeus Serenus.
the story of Marcus weeping comes from a perfectly reliable source
it's from a late Roman history that scholars treat with caution.

games.q: young Marcus weeps for his tutor, and courtiers try to stop him. what does the emperor Antoninus say, in the story?
o: a future emperor must not cry.
games.why: the story says Antoninus told them neither philosophy nor empire takes away natural feeling.

practice: Find one feeling that's actually here right now, tiredness, sadness, hope, relief, anything, and name it quietly.

Instead of managing it, let it be felt fully, the way you'd let a wave reach the shore: where is it in your body, and how big is it, really? Stay with it, breathing, not pushing it away and not feeding it.

wordCard.voice: Apatheia, the Stoics' ideal of freedom from runaway passions, not from feeling: honest tears, and a steady center.

orig.note: Greek: freedom from passions; not the same as English apathy.

carryVoice: Your line: not unfeeling. A Stoic can cry, and still stand steady. Day two hundred ninety-eight, done.

sources.ref: Historia Augusta, Life of Antoninus Pius 10.5
